To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

H-ras mutations are detected in a small sub-populations of mouse liver tumors that are initiated by other genetic alterations and that H-ras mutation is more frequent in tumors that are histologically benign than in tumors that are malignant

a specific point mutation can be present as a primary or as a secondary event in the progression of a tumor and that the frequency with which a specific mutation is present as a primary event in a tumor depends on the mutation rate for that target site.
the same oncogene mutation that is identified as a tumor initiating event can also occur during the subsequent development of the tumor as a secondary event.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of new molecular genetic techniques for the study of tumor progression in the mouse liver.

the molecular mechanisms that lead to tumor development in the mouse liver and with the development of molecular methods for the detection of mutations that occur during mouse liver tumor development.
the development of a novel genotypic selection technique for the detection of specific point mutations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mutations are present at all stages of tumor progression.
a mutation is present in a tumor when it is detected at a level of 1% of the tumor cells.
the mutation was a tumor-initiating mutation in 13 of the 21 tumors and a secondary event in 8 of the 21.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the occurrence of a mutation in a tumor as an initiating or secondary event is dependent on the mutation rate for the site and the number of cell divisions that occur before the mutation is fixed in a cell population.
the occurrence of a mutation during tumor progression can be detected at low mutant fractions by using ACB-PCR.
the mutation rate for the H-rab codon 61 mutation in the mouse liver is approximately 10(-5) per cell per generation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mutation rate for a target site can vary by orders of magnitude depending on the cell type and the type of DNA damage.
the occurrence of a mutation during tumor development may not reflect the mutation rate for that target sequence.
the occurrence of a mutation at any stage during tumor progression is not necessarily an indication that it was the initiating event.
